listening.title: Riverside Clinic Reminder Trial Call
listening.focus: appointment details, time correction and reminder arrangements
listening.script:
Sarah: Good morning, Riverside Public Clinic, Sarah speaking, how can I help?
David: Hi, it's David Chen, I have an appointment next Tuesday and I got a text about a reminder trial?
Sarah: Yes, David, I can see you. You're booked for Tuesday the 14th with Dr. Patel. Originally at 10:30, sorry, I mean 11:30, the morning clinic was moved an hour later.
David: Oh, 11:30, not 10:30? Thanks for letting me know.
Sarah: Yes, 11:30 in Room 3. We're testing two reminder types. You already received an SMS yesterday, did you get it?
David: Yes, at about 4 pm.
Sarah: Great. That message asks you to reply YES to confirm, or you can just confirm when we call you the day before. Either way is fine.
David: So I don't have to reply if you call?
Sarah: Exactly, one confirmation is enough. If you reply YES now, we won't call. If not, we'll phone Monday afternoon.
David: I think I'll wait for the call, easier for me.
Sarah: No problem. Also, please bring your health card and arrive 15 minutes early to update your details. Also, parking at the clinic is limited. The trial information sheet suggests using the bus, but the car park on Mill Street is free for patients for two hours if you bring your ticket to reception.
David: Good to know, I'll probably take the bus anyway.
Sarah: That's probably quicker. The number 42 stops right outside.
David: And is there any cost for the appointment?
Sarah: No, it's fully covered. The reminder trial is free as well.
Sarah: Perfect. One more thing, the trial also sends a follow-up message after the visit to check if the reminder was helpful. You can ignore it if you want.
David: Okay, thanks for explaining everything.
Sarah: Thank you, David. See you Tuesday at 11:30.

reading.title: Central Park Accessibility Audit
reading.focus: audit methods, access barriers and planned improvements
reading.passage:
The city council carried out an accessibility audit of Central Park in March to check how easy the park is for all visitors, including wheelchair users, parents with pushchairs, and people with low vision. Two trained auditors visited on weekdays and weekends, and they also spoke to 40 regular park users. The aim was to identify barriers and suggest low-cost improvements.

The audit found clear progress since 2021. The north entrance now has a wide, flat ramp with handrails, and the main paths from there to the café and toilets are smooth and wide enough for two wheelchairs to pass. Signs along these paths use large print and simple symbols, which most users said were helpful. The council report claims that these changes show a strong commitment to inclusion.

However, problems remain in other areas. The south entrance still has only steps, with no alternative flat route, so visitors who cannot use steps must make a long detour to the north side. Inside the park, the path to the lake is narrow, uneven, and often blocked by tree roots, making it difficult for wheelchairs and pushchairs. The audit noted that this was the most common complaint in interviews.

Facilities were mixed. The new accessible toilet near the café was clean, well signed, and had enough space for a wheelchair and a helper. In contrast, the older toilets by the playground were small, poorly lit, and lacked support rails. The playground itself has one inclusive swing, but the surface around it is soft sand, which wheelchairs cannot cross easily. As an example of good practice, the auditors praised the staff at the café, who offered help with carrying trays and reading menus aloud.

Information was also uneven. The main noticeboard at the north entrance lists accessible routes in three languages, while the small board at the south entrance is out of date and hard to read. Auditors suggested standardising signs across the park.

Overall, the report concludes that Central Park is becoming more welcoming, but access is still unequal. Visitors who enter from the north and stay on the main paths have a positive experience, while those who use the south side or want to reach the lake face significant barriers. The council plans to add a ramp at the south entrance and resurface the lake path next year, subject to funding. Funding will be decided in November, and work could start in spring if approved.

exercises.title: Central Park Accessibility Audit
exercises.focus: audit methods, access barriers and planned improvements
exercises.passage:
The city council carried out an accessibility audit of Central Park in March to check how easy the park is for all visitors, including wheelchair users, parents with pushchairs, and people with low vision. Two trained auditors visited on weekdays and weekends, and they also spoke to 40 regular park users. The aim was to identify barriers and suggest low-cost improvements.

The audit found clear progress since 2021. The north entrance now has a wide, flat ramp with handrails, and the main paths from there to the café and toilets are smooth and wide enough for two wheelchairs to pass. Signs along these paths use large print and simple symbols, which most users said were helpful. The council report claims that these changes show a strong commitment to inclusion.

However, problems remain in other areas. The south entrance still has only steps, with no alternative flat route, so visitors who cannot use steps must make a long detour to the north side. Inside the park, the path to the lake is narrow, uneven, and often blocked by tree roots, making it difficult for wheelchairs and pushchairs. The audit noted that this was the most common complaint in interviews.

Facilities were mixed. The new accessible toilet near the café was clean, well signed, and had enough space for a wheelchair and a helper. In contrast, the older toilets by the playground were small, poorly lit, and lacked support rails. The playground itself has one inclusive swing, but the surface around it is soft sand, which wheelchairs cannot cross easily. As an example of good practice, the auditors praised the staff at the café, who offered help with carrying trays and reading menus aloud.

Information was also uneven. The main noticeboard at the north entrance lists accessible routes in three languages, while the small board at the south entrance is out of date and hard to read. Auditors suggested standardising signs across the park.

Overall, the report concludes that Central Park is becoming more welcoming, but access is still unequal. Visitors who enter from the north and stay on the main paths have a positive experience, while those who use the south side or want to reach the lake face significant barriers. The council plans to add a ramp at the south entrance and resurface the lake path next year, subject to funding. Funding will be decided in November, and work could start in spring if approved.
exercises.prompt: Why did the council carry out the audit?
options: To check ease of use for all visitors
To close the south entrance permanently
To build a new café and toilets
To train 40 regular park users
exercises.explanation: The passage states the aim was to check ease for all visitors. Option D confuses the interview sample with the purpose.

writingPrompts.focus: Presenting linked ideas and a clear position with support
writingPrompts.prompt:
Some people think that projects at a college showcase should be judged only by teachers, while others believe that students and visitors should also have a vote.
Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
Write at least 250 words.

writingPrompts.task: Task 2 · Community Health-Information Evenings and Online Information
writingPrompts.prompt:
Some people believe that community health-information evenings are one of the best ways to help people stay healthy, while others think that getting health information online is more practical and useful.
Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
Write at least 250 words.

writingPrompts.task: Task 2 · Compulsory Park Volunteering for Students
writingPrompts.focus: Explaining advantages and disadvantages with linked examples
writingPrompts.prompt:
Some colleges require students to complete a number of volunteer hours in local parks, for example helping with planting, cleaning, or guiding visitors.
What are the advantages and disadvantages of this requirement?
Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
Write at least 250 words.

speakingPrompts.focus: Paraphrasing familiar answers and linking ideas
speakingPrompts.prompt:
Let's talk about health and daily routines.
- What do you usually do to stay healthy?
- Where do you prefer to get information about health?
- Have your health habits changed compared to a few years ago?
- Do you think community events can help people learn about health?

Let's talk about your studies and college life.
- What kind of projects do you enjoy working on?
- Do you prefer working alone or with other students?
- Have you ever shown your work to other people? How did you feel?
- What do you think makes a good project presentation?

speakingPrompts.focus: Describing an event with linked details and clear sequencing
speakingPrompts.prompt:
Describe a community health-information evening, college project showcase, or park volunteer activity you attended or heard about.
You should say:
- when and where it took place
- what happened during the event
- who organised it or who you went with
- and explain what you learned from it or why it was memorable.
You will have one minute to prepare and should speak for one to two minutes.

speakingPrompts.focus: Giving reasons and evaluating different approaches
speakingPrompts.prompt:
Let's discuss community learning events.
- Why do some people attend community health or education evenings while others do not?
- What makes a community event more useful than simply reading information online?
- How can organisers make sure information is accurate and easy to understand?
- Do you think local events will become more or less important in the future? Why?

speakingPrompts.focus: Comparing views and justifying opinions about volunteering
